title: Shapes and Patterns: Triangles, Quadrilaterals and Patterns
seo_title: Triangles, Quadrilaterals and Patterns Class 5 Worksheet with Answers (Maths Mela Chapter 7)
standard_code: Class 5, Maths Mela Chapter 7: Shapes and Patterns
standard_text: Shapes and patterns: properties of triangles and quadrilaterals, tiling patterns, and number and shape patterns with rules (summary of NCERT Maths Mela Class 5)
meta_desc: Class 5 Shapes and Patterns worksheet (Maths Mela Chapter 7): triangles, quadrilaterals, angle sums, growing patterns and rules. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Angles in a triangle add up to 180°.
key_sub: Find the rule to continue a pattern.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Triangles: equilateral (3 equal sides), isosceles (2 equal), scalene (none). Angles add up to 180°.
  • Quadrilaterals: square, rectangle, parallelogram, rhombus, trapezium.
  • A growing pattern follows a rule: +3 each step.

Examples

Example

Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 60°.

180° − 110°

Answer: 70°

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Using 360° for a triangleA triangle's angles add up to 180°.
Thinking a rhombus has right anglesOnly a square rhombus does.

faq.a: A triangle with two equal sides (and two equal angles).
A pattern that changes by the same rule each step.

items.q: Which is the best name for this triangle?
items.e: Two sides have tick marks, so exactly 2 sides are equal. It has no right angle. It is an isosceles triangle. The base has no tick mark.

items.q: Which is the best name for this triangle?
items.e: All 3 sides have tick marks, so all 3 sides are equal. It is an equilateral triangle. Pointing down does not change its name.

items.q: Which is the best name for this triangle?
items.e: The small square marks a right angle (90°). No sides are equal, so it is a right-angled triangle.

items.q: Which is the best name for this triangle?
items.e: It has a right angle (the small square) and 2 equal sides (tick marks), so it is a right-angled isosceles triangle. The 2 equal sides are the arms of the right angle.

items.q: Which is the best name for this triangle?
items.e: Two sides have tick marks, so exactly 2 sides are equal. It has no right angle. It is an isosceles triangle. It lies on its side, but 2 sides still have tick marks. Turning a triangle never changes its name.

items.q: Which is the best name for this triangle?
items.e: The small square marks a right angle (90°). No sides are equal, so it is a right-angled triangle. It is turned, but the small square still shows the right angle.

items.q: Which is the best name for this triangle?
items.e: It has a right angle (the small square) and 2 equal sides (tick marks), so it is a right-angled isosceles triangle. It is turned, but the marks do not change.

items.q: Which is the best name for this triangle?
items.e: All 3 sides have tick marks, so all 3 sides are equal. It is an equilateral triangle. It is turned on its side, but all 3 sides are still equal.

items.q: Which is the best name for this triangle?
items.e: Two sides are 6 cm, so exactly 2 sides are equal. The equal sides do not have to be the slanted ones.

items.q: Which is the best name for this triangle?
items.e: All 3 sides are 5 cm.

items.q: Which is the best name for this triangle?
items.e: Two sides are 7.5 cm. It points down, but it is still isosceles.

items.q: Which triangle is an isosceles triangle?
items.e: Triangle B has tick marks on 2 sides, so it is isosceles, even though it points down. The other triangles have no equal sides.

items.q: Which triangle is a right-angled triangle?
items.e: Triangle C has a small square in one corner, so one angle is 90°. It is turned, but it is still right-angled.

items.q: Which triangle is an equilateral triangle?
items.e: Triangle D has tick marks on all 3 sides. The other triangles have only 2 equal sides.

items.q: A triangle has sides of 8 cm, 8 cm and 5 cm. What type of triangle is it?
items.e: Two sides are 8 cm, so exactly 2 sides are equal. It is an isosceles triangle.

items.q: What do the tick marks on the sides of a triangle show?
items.e: Sides with the same tick marks have the same length. A small square, not a tick mark, shows a right angle.

items.q: An equilateral triangle has a perimeter of 27 cm. How long is each side?
items.e: All 3 sides are equal: 27 ÷ 3 = 9 cm. (13.5 cm is 27 ÷ 2, and 81 cm is 27 × 3.)

items.q: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 20 cm. Its two equal sides are 7 cm each. How long is the third side?
items.e: 7 + 7 = 14 cm. 20 − 14 = 6 cm. (13 cm takes away only one of the 7 cm sides.)

items.q: Gauri says a right-angled triangle can also be an isosceles triangle. Is she correct?
c: No, it must have 3 equal sides
No, it can only have one name
items.e: A right-angled triangle with 2 equal sides is a right-angled isosceles triangle, like half of a square cut along a diagonal.

items.q: Rehan says a triangle is isosceles only if it points up. Is he correct?
c: No, it can point any way
items.e: The name depends only on the sides. Turning an isosceles triangle does not change its 2 equal sides.

items.q: The three angles of any triangle add up to
items.e: The angles of every triangle add up to 180°. (360° is the total for a four-sided figure such as a square.)

items.q: Find ∠x.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 50° + 60° = 110°, and 180° − 110° = 70°. Subtract both known angles, not just one.

items.q: Find ∠x.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 35° + 70° = 105°, and 180° − 105° = 75°. Subtract both known angles, not just one.

items.q: Find ∠x.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 25° + 115° = 140°, and 180° − 140° = 40°. Subtract both known angles, not just one.

items.q: Find ∠x.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 64° + 72° = 136°, and 180° − 136° = 44°. Subtract both known angles, not just one.

items.q: Find ∠x.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 45° + 105° = 150°, and 180° − 150° = 30°. Subtract both known angles, not just one.

items.q: Find ∠x.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 55° + 77° = 132°, and 180° − 132° = 48°. Subtract both known angles, not just one.

items.q: Find ∠PRQ.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 48° + 62° = 110°, and 180° − 110° = 70°.

items.q: Find ∠LKM.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 34° + 46° = 80°, and 180° − 80° = 100°.

items.q: Find ∠DEF.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 57° + 52° = 109°, and 180° − 109° = 71°.

items.q: In triangle PQR, ∠P = 47° and ∠Q = 68°. Find ∠R.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 47° + 68° = 115°, and 180° − 115° = 65°.

items.q: In triangle ABC, ∠A = 112° and ∠B = 29°. Find ∠C.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 112° + 29° = 141°, and 180° − 141° = 39°.

items.q: In triangle XYZ, ∠X = 38° and ∠Z = 85°. Find ∠Y.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 38° + 85° = 123°, and 180° − 123° = 57°.

items.q: Two angles of a triangle are 73° and 54°. What is the third angle?
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 73° + 54° = 127°, and 180° − 127° = 53°.

items.q: Two angles of a triangle are 26° and 19°. What is the third angle?
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 26° + 19° = 45°, and 180° − 45° = 135°.

items.q: Which set of angles can be the three angles of a triangle?
items.e: 50° + 60° + 70° = 180°, so these angles work. The others do not add up to 180°: 50°, 60°, 80° add up to 190°; 90°, 45°, 55° add up to 190°; 100°, 50°, 40° add up to 190°.

items.q: Which set of angles can be the three angles of a triangle?
items.e: 35° + 65° + 80° = 180°, so these angles work. The others do not add up to 180°: 35°, 65°, 90° add up to 190°; 60°, 60°, 70° add up to 190°; 120°, 30°, 40° add up to 190°.

items.q: Nikhil draws a big triangle and a small triangle. He says the angles of the big triangle add up to more. Is he correct?
c: No, the small one has more
items.e: The angles of every triangle add up to 180°, big or small. A bigger triangle has longer sides, not bigger angles.

items.q: Shreya tears off the 3 corners of a paper triangle and puts them together, point to point. What do they make?
items.e: The 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180°, so the 3 corners fit together to make a straight line.

items.q: Can a triangle have angles of 95° and 85°?
items.e: 95° + 85° = 180°. That leaves 0° for the third angle, so these cannot be two angles of a triangle.

items.q: A quadrilateral has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles. Is it a rhombus?
items.e: It has 4 equal sides, so it is a rhombus. With 4 right angles it is a special rhombus called a square.

items.q: What is the best name for this figure? Use the marks.
items.e: The arrows show exactly 1 pair of parallel sides. The other 2 sides are not parallel, so it is a trapezium. Turning a figure does not change its name.

items.q: What is the best name for this figure? Use the marks.
items.e: The arrows show exactly 1 pair of parallel sides. The other 2 sides are not parallel, so it is a trapezium. Turning a figure does not change its name.

items.q: A rhombus is a parallelogram with ______.
items.e: A rhombus has 2 pairs of parallel sides like every parallelogram, and all 4 of its sides are equal. It does not need right angles; that would make it a square.

items.q: What is the best name for this figure? Use the marks.
items.e: The arrows show exactly 1 pair of parallel sides. The other 2 sides are not parallel, so it is a trapezium.

items.q: How many pairs of parallel sides does a parallelogram have?
items.e: Both pairs of opposite sides of a parallelogram are parallel: 2 pairs.

items.q: What is the best name for this figure? Use the marks.
items.e: The tick marks show 4 equal sides, so it is a rhombus. It has no right angles, so it is not a square. Turning a figure does not change its name.

items.q: Which figure has 4 equal sides but no right angles?
items.e: Figure B is a rhombus: 4 equal sides and no right angles. The square also has 4 equal sides, but it has 4 right angles.

items.q: What is the best name for this figure? Use the marks.
items.e: The tick marks show 4 equal sides, so it is a rhombus. It has no right angles, so it is not a square.

items.q: A quadrilateral has 2 pairs of parallel sides. Its sides are not all equal and it has no right angles. What is its best name?
items.e: 2 pairs of parallel sides make a parallelogram. Its sides are not all equal, so it is not a rhombus or a square.

items.q: Which property does a parallelogram have that a trapezium does not?
items.e: A trapezium has exactly 1 pair of parallel sides. A parallelogram has 2 pairs.

items.q: ABCD is a parallelogram. AB = 9 cm and AD = 5 cm. Find its perimeter.
items.e: Opposite sides are equal, so the sides are 9 cm, 5 cm, 9 cm and 5 cm. Perimeter = 9 + 5 + 9 + 5 = 28 cm.

items.q: ABCD is a parallelogram. Which two angles are equal?
items.e: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal. ∠B and ∠D are opposite each other. Angles next to each other, such as ∠A and ∠B, add up to 180°.

items.q: ABCD is a parallelogram. Find ∠x.
items.e: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal. ∠x is opposite ∠ABC, so ∠x = 118°.

items.q: Which property does a rhombus have that a parallelogram does not always have?
items.e: Every parallelogram has parallel and equal opposite sides and equal opposite angles. Only a rhombus must have all 4 sides equal.

items.q: ABCD is a rhombus. AB = 8 cm. Find its perimeter.
items.e: All 4 sides of a rhombus are equal. Perimeter = 4 × 8 = 32 cm.

items.q: ABCD is a trapezium. AB ∥ DC. Which two angles must add up to 180°?
items.e: ∠A and ∠D are at the two ends of side AD, between the parallel sides AB and DC, so they add up to 180°. ∠A and ∠B are on the same parallel side, so they do not.

items.q: ABCD is a parallelogram. AB = 12 cm and BC = 7 cm. Find the length of CD.
items.e: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal. CD is opposite AB, so CD = 12 cm.

items.q: PQRS is a trapezium. PQ ∥ SR and ∠P = 80°. Which angle must be 100°?
items.e: ∠P and ∠S are at the two ends of side PS, between the parallel sides PQ and SR. They add up to 180°, so ∠S = 180° − 80° = 100°.

items.q: ABCD is a trapezium. AB ∥ DC. Find ∠x.
items.e: ∠ABC and ∠x lie between the parallel sides AB and DC, on the same side BC, so they add up to 180°. ∠x = 180° − 48° = 132°.

items.q:
What is the next term?
6, 10, 14, 18, ?
items.e: The pattern grows by 4 each time (6 + 4 = 10). Next: 18 + 4 = 22.

items.q:
What is the next term?
15, 23, 31, 39, ?
items.e: The pattern grows by 8 each time (15 + 8 = 23). Next: 39 + 8 = 47.

items.q:
What is the next term?
120, 145, 170, 195, ?
items.e: The pattern grows by 25 each time (120 + 25 = 145). Next: 195 + 25 = 220.

items.q:
What is the next term?
150, 138, 126, 114, ?
items.e: The pattern shrinks by 12 each time (150 − 12 = 138). Next: 114 − 12 = 102.

items.q:
What is the next term?
1,000, 875, 750, 625, ?
items.e: The pattern shrinks by 125 each time (1,000 − 125 = 875). Next: 625 − 125 = 500.

items.q:
What is the next term?
90, 84, 78, 72, ?
items.e: The pattern shrinks by 6 each time (90 − 6 = 84). Next: 72 − 6 = 66.

items.q:
What is the next term?
75, 70, 65, 60, ?
items.e: The pattern shrinks by 5 each time (75 − 5 = 70). Next: 60 − 5 = 55.

items.q:
What is the next term?
640, 320, 160, 80, ?
items.e: Each term is half of the one before (divide by 2): 80 ÷ 2 = 40. (Subtracting 320 like the first step does not work after that.)

items.q:
What is the next term?
1, 2, 4, 7, 11, ?
items.e: The jumps are 1, 2, 3, 4, so the next jump is 5: 11 + 5 = 16. (Adding the first jump gives 12.)

items.q:
What is the next term?
2, 6, 18, 54, ?
items.e: Each term is 3 times the one before: 54 × 3 = 162. (Adding the first jump, 54 + 4 = 58, only works for the first step.)

items.q:
What is the next term?
3, 6, 12, 24, ?
items.e: The jumps are 3, 6, 12, so the pattern does not add the same amount. Each term is 2 times the one before: 24 × 2 = 48. (Adding the first jump, 24 + 3 = 27, only works for the first step.)

items.q:
What is the missing term?
35, 50, ?, 80, 95
items.e: The pattern grows by 15 each time. The missing term is 50 + 15 = 65. Check: 65 + 15 = 80.

items.q:
What is the missing term?
8, ?, 20, 26, 32
items.e: The pattern grows by 6 each time. The missing term is 8 + 6 = 14. Check: 14 + 6 = 20. (The jump from 8 to 20 is 12, but the missing term sits halfway between them.)

items.q:
What is the missing term?
100, 92, ?, 76, 68
items.e: The pattern shrinks by 8 each time. The missing term is 92 − 8 = 84. Check: 84 − 8 = 76.

items.q:
What is the missing term?
4,500, 5,000, 5,500, ?, 6,500
items.e: The pattern grows by 500 each time. The missing term is 5,500 + 500 = 6,000. Check: 6,000 + 500 = 6,500.

items.q: The pattern continues. How many craft sticks will Figure 4 need?
items.e: Count each figure: 4, 7, 10. Each figure adds 3 craft sticks. Figure 4: 10 + 3 = 13.

items.q: The pattern continues. How many tiles will Figure 4 need?
items.e: Count each figure: 4, 6, 8. Each figure adds 2 tiles. Figure 4: 8 + 2 = 10.

items.q: The pattern continues. How many craft sticks will Figure 4 need?
items.e: Count each figure: 6, 11, 16. Each figure adds 5 craft sticks. Figure 4: 16 + 5 = 21.

items.q: The pattern continues. How many tiles will Figure 4 need?
items.e: Count each figure: 3, 5, 7. Each figure adds 2 tiles. Figure 4: 7 + 2 = 9.

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
4, 8, 12, 16, …
c: Start at 4 and add 4 each time.
Start at 4 and multiply by 2 each time.
Start at 4 and add 8 each time.
Start at 8 and add 4 each time.
items.e: Each term is 4 more than the one before. “Multiply by 2” works for 4 → 8 but not for 8 → 12.

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
100, 93, 86, 79, …
c: Start at 100 and subtract 7 each time.
Start at 79 and subtract 7 each time.
Start at 100 and add 7 each time.
Start at 93 and subtract 7 each time.
items.e: The first term is 100, and each term is 7 less than the one before: 100 − 7 = 93, 93 − 7 = 86.

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
96, 48, 24, 12, …
c: Start at 96 and subtract 48 each time.
Start at 48 and divide by 2 each time.
Start at 96 and subtract 24 each time.
Start at 96 and divide by 2 each time.
items.e: Each term is half of the one before: 96 ÷ 2 = 48, 48 ÷ 2 = 24, 24 ÷ 2 = 12. “Subtract 48” works only for the first step.

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
3, 9, 15, 21, …
c: Start at 3 and add 6 each time.
Start at 9 and add 6 each time.
Start at 3 and multiply by 3 each time.
Start at 6 and add 3 each time.
items.e: Each term is 6 more than the one before. “Multiply by 3” works for 3 → 9 but not for 9 → 15.

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
2, 4, 8, 16, …
c: Start at 2 and multiply by 2 each time.
Start at 2 and add 4 each time.
Start at 4 and multiply by 2 each time.
Start at 2 and add 2 each time.
items.e: Each term is 2 times the one before: 2 × 2 = 4, 4 × 2 = 8, 8 × 2 = 16. “Add 2” works only for the first step.

items.q: Which rule gives the term value from the term number?
items.e: The term value goes up by 2, so multiply the term number by 2. Term 1: 1 × 2 = 2, and the value is 7, so add 5. Check term 4: 4 × 2 + 5 = 13. (A rule must work for every term, not only term 1.)

items.q: Which rule gives the term value from the term number?
items.e: The term value goes up by 3, so multiply the term number by 3. Term 1: 1 × 3 = 3, and the value is 4, so add 1. Check term 4: 4 × 3 + 1 = 13. (A rule must work for every term, not only term 1.)

items.q: Which rule gives the term value from the term number?
items.e: The term value goes up by 4, so multiply the term number by 4. Term 1: 1 × 4 = 4, and the value is 7, so add 3. Check term 4: 4 × 4 + 3 = 19. (A rule must work for every term, not only term 1.)

items.q: Which rule gives the term value from the term number?
items.e: The term value goes up by 5, so multiply the term number by 5. Term 1: 1 × 5 = 5, and the value is 3, so subtract 2. Check term 4: 4 × 5 − 2 = 18. (A rule must work for every term, not only term 1.)

items.q: Which rule gives the term value from the term number?
items.e: The term value goes up by 10, so multiply the term number by 10. Term 1: 1 × 10 = 10, and the value is 15, so add 5. Check term 4: 4 × 10 + 5 = 45. (A rule must work for every term, not only term 1.)

items.q: What is the missing term value?
items.e: The term value goes up by 7 each time. 30 + 7 = 37.

items.q: What is the missing term value?
items.e: The term value goes up by 3 each time. 11 + 3 = 14.

items.q: What is the missing term value?
items.e: The term value goes up by 5 each time. 17 + 5 = 22.

items.q: What is the missing term value?
items.e: The term value goes down by 5 each time. 50 − 5 = 45.

items.q: What is the missing term value?
items.e: The term value goes up by 4 each time. 18 + 4 = 22.

items.q: The pattern continues in the same way. What is the term value for term number 8?
items.e: From term 1 to term 8 there are 7 jumps of 8: 90 − 7 × 8 = 90 − 56 = 34. (58 is the value for term 5, the next term in the list.)

items.q: The pattern continues in the same way. What is the term value for term number 8?
items.e: From term 1 to term 8 there are 7 jumps of 3: 5 + 7 × 3 = 5 + 21 = 26. (17 is the value for term 5, the next term in the list.)

items.q: The pattern continues in the same way. What is the term value for term number 12?
items.e: From term 1 to term 12 there are 11 jumps of 5: 2 + 11 × 5 = 2 + 55 = 57. (22 is the value for term 5, the next term in the list.)

items.q: The pattern continues in the same way. What is the term value for term number 10?
items.e: From term 1 to term 10 there are 9 jumps of 6: 100 − 9 × 6 = 100 − 54 = 46. (76 is the value for term 5, the next term in the list.)

items.q: The pattern continues in the same way. What is the term value for term number 10?
items.e: From term 1 to term 10 there are 9 jumps of 4: 6 + 9 × 4 = 6 + 36 = 42. (22 is the value for term 5, the next term in the list.)
